description_full: Nathan's Famous, Inc., along with its subsidiaries, operates in the foodservice industry both in the United States and internationally. It operates through three segments: Branded Product Program; Product licensing; and Restaurant operations. The company owns and franchises restaurants under the Nathan's Famous brand name. It also has license agreements for the manufacture, distribution, marketing, and sale of Nathan's Famous branded beef hot dogs, crinkle-cut french fries, and sausages in refrigerated consumer packages, which are resold through retail channels such as supermarkets, grocery stores, mass merchandisers, and club stores. In addition, the company has license agreements to manufacture Nathan's Famous branded hot dog and sausage products in bulk for use in the foodservice industry, supply Nathan's Famous natural casing and skinless hot dogs in bulk for use in the Nathan's Famous restaurant system, as well as manufacture proprietary spices; produce and distribute pickles; and produce and sell french fries and onion rings for retail sale. Further, the company produces and sells miniature bagel dogs, franks-in-a-blanket, mozzarella sticks, corn dog nuggets, other hors d'oeuvres, and bottled mustard through club stores, supermarkets, and other retail food stores. Additionally, it sells Nathan's products directly to foodservice operators or various foodservice distributors, and provides Fish-n-Chips under the Arthur Treacher's brand name. Nathan's Famous, Inc. was founded in 1916 and is headquartered in Jericho, New York. As of October 26, 2026, Nathan's Famous, Inc. operates as a subsidiary of Smithfield Foods, Inc.

financial_summary: Nathan's Famous, Inc. is a small-cap consumer cyclical business with a $418M market cap on $162M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 455% against a 7% cost of capital — a 448-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 37%.

The business throws off $18M in free cash flow — roughly 11 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.91× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.8× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 10.5×.

Shareholder yield of 4.4% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 30% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.3× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 19% operating margin runs 11pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (8%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.25x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+6.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 8% below the high.
With a beta of 0.56, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.12 vs 5y 0.46), so read it loosely.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $95.63 (margin of safety -7%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 33%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $74.00 to $129 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/FCF 23.4 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 5.2% annual cash-flow growth, 1pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 455% clears the cost of capital of 7.2% by 448pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.80).
It runs a 37% gross margin and converts 11% of revenue into free cash flow.
It spends 0.7% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.8x net debt to EBITDA ($24.4M of cash against $48.1M of debt), with interest covered 10.5x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 9.4, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.4% over 3 years, 16.4% over 5 years and 5.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 16%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 9.8% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 0% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 30%.
Capex runs only 0.4x depreciation (0.2% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 27, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 30.0%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 57%.
It returns 4.4% a year to shareholders (2.0% in dividends).
people: With about 129 employees, each generates about $1.3M of revenue, 3.3x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 6.1% a year.
That works out to $138K of free cash flow per employee.
